facts.raw_span: asymptomatic erythematous scaly plaques over the face and proximal extremities
involvement of the upper respiratory tract, causing palatal perforation and stridor, necessitating a tracheostomy a year ago
no history of preceding trauma, fever, malaise, joint pain, cough, epistaxis, hemoptysis, or hematuria
multiple well-defined brown erythematous scaly plaques with central scarring measuring 2 × 1 to 8 × 7 cm on the face, arm, and thighs
saddle nose deformity, perforation of the hard palate, and necrotic plaques on the ear with destruction of ear cartilage
cervical lymphadenopathy: multiple, nontender, discrete nodes, ranging from 1.5 to 2 cm without surface changes
anemia (hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL)
normal kidney function test
normal liver function test
infiltrate of foamy histiocytes and pigmented yeasts without multiaxial septation (Fontana-Masson)
pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, parakeratosis, dense dermal infiltrate of histiocytes, foamy histiocytes, neutrophils, and multinucleate giant cells along with pigmented hyphae
fungal skin culture: black yeastlike colonies characteristic of Exophiala spinifera species

concepts.why: The presence of pigmented yeasts without multiaxial septation and pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, along with the fungal skin culture results, support this diagnosis.
The patient's saddle nose deformity is a result of the destructive nature of the underlying disease process.
The patient's history of upper respiratory tract involvement and tracheostomy suggests a severe disease process affecting the palate.
The patient's cervical lymphadenopathy is likely a response to the underlying infection or disease process.
The patient's anemia may be a result of chronic disease or infection, which can lead to inflammation and decreased red blood cell production.
The fungal skin culture results confirm the presence of Exophiala spinifera, a type of black yeastlike fungus.
The patient's histopathology results show a dense dermal infiltrate of histiocytes, foamy histiocytes, neutrophils, and multinucleate giant cells, consistent with a destructive granuloma.
The patient's clinical presentation and laboratory results suggest a chronic fungal infection, which has led to significant tissue destruction and morbidity.
